Money vs Medals

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
how do professional athletes survive in South Africa?

Summary:
South Africa's medal tally at the Olympic and Commonwealth Games seems to be a hit and miss affair. With more money going to the Lovelife campaign than all the sporting codes combined, it seems our athletes attain success in spite of not because of government support and Lotto handouts.

Further information:
SASCOC has an annual funding programme for elite athletes, but how much do they get and is it enough? Why are some of our top performers trying to make a future in the US? And once our athletes attain gold, are we rewarding them sufficiently?

Extra Budget Items:
Flights to Cape Town to interview Ryk Neethling and the Minister of Sport and Recreation, Mbalula Fikile.

Press Release:


Money or medals?
Only hours of gruelling training and commitment will see them join the ranks of the world’s super athletes. But despite the fact that South Africa’s top Olympic athletes live, train and compete on shoestring budgets well below what their international peers earn, their spirit is unwavering. Carte Blanche meets the Olympic hopefuls who sacrifice all for dreams of gold and glory.


Script:


MONEY VS MEDALS

V/O: It’s 7.00am at Roodeplaat Dam just outside Pretoria. The South African rowing team is preparing for the early morning training session. The creaking of boats and the gentle camaraderie is a daily ritual shared by this tight knit group.

Devi link: The 2016 Olympics in Rio is just around the corner, and thousands of athletes around the world are preparing to chase that dream for a gold medal. But what exactly does it take to make that dream come true?

Roger: You know one thing saying I want to win Olympic gold, the next thing is now arrive on my doorstep every day for the next 3 years – and when I say every day it’s not Monday to Friday, it’s Monday to Sunday – from now until Christmas. I give the athletes 3 weeks off a year, apart from that they’re training. We train as a squad every day, so it’s a massive commitment from their side.

V/O: Roger Barrow is the national coach, who has managed to produce a culture of excellence on a fraction of the resources needed. By consulting widely to create a world-class rowing programme, he’s achieved phenomenal results with this gifted young team.
Roger: We’ve got an elite team of 12 athletes. In that 12 are my top team to contend for Rio. In that team we’ve got James Thompson, John Smith and Lawrence Ndlovu who were from the Olympic foursome that won Olympic gold.

V/O: In what was called the greatest rowing finish the Olympics has ever seen, the South Africans snatched gold at London 2012 by a quarter of a second.

Roger: After 2012 when we won Olympic gold, as a coach I really thought that our sport was going to come into the limelight and we’d be recognized like athletics and swimming, but to my disappointment nothing really changed.

V/O: Rowing receives almost no television coverage and the athletes like James Thompson remain virtually unknown. Not that he’s complaining. He and his teammates are quietly getting on with the job at hand.

James: My average day starts at 5.20 every morning, I get to Roodeplaat Dam by 7am every morning, we are here until about 9.30, and then we head back to the HPC. We normally have an Ergo in the middle of the day, or gym like today.

Devi: Ergo?

James: A rowing machine. A rowing ergo, and that will be another 90 minutes on that probably.

V/O: The athletes always train together as a squad, not on their own. They have a partnership with the High Performance Centre at Pretoria University with instant access to doctors, physiotherapists and specialist strength coaching. The day ends after 4pm, but once a week they get the afternoon off, and James goes to his part-time job as a marketing intern.

James: Thursday afternoons are fantastic. I have to go to the office try and earn a crust of bread, and then I work remotely as much as I can between training sessions.

Devi: That can’t be easy just looking at your schedule?

James: It isn’t easy, but it doesn’t have to be easy, it has to be fast.

V/O: And James is the fastest in the world. In 2014 he and team mate John Smith bagged gold in the lightweight double sculls at the World Championships in Amsterdam. In a thrilling finish, they beat France by 1/100th of a second to become South Africa’s first World Championship gold medalists. Not only are they Olympic and world champions, they are also the world record holders.

Sfx: “French team just trying to dig in but it is ooh, the South Africans I think!”

V/O: This was a "medal by design", the result of a focused project, proving how high-performance sport should work. The 12 South African rowers are all ranked within the top 5 in the world. But what do they earn?
Devi: Is the team funded?
James: A lot of the senior athletes are funded by Sascoc and Sascoc has certainly kept my dream alive. A lot of people are critical of them, but my dream in London would certainly not have happened without Sascoc.

V/O: SASCOC has a programme called Operation Excellence which pays a stipend to 67 of the top performing athletes in the country.

James: They cover my petrol, they cover my medical aid, my cellphone, my groceries. I get about R8500 a month if I can provide slips to show that’s where the money’s been spent.

V/O: At 28 years old, James is clearly earning far less than his peers.

James: I'm getting by month to month. I've been very grateful to have had the support of my parents before I was a senior, and to a degree my wife at the moment. But I don't have a retirement fund, I'm fearful every time my car has to go for a service, but at the same time it's a passion, and it’s a dream and I will chase the Rio dream all the way to Rio.

Devi: I know Sascoc gives money to individual rowers, but what about the entire team?

Roger: So the team they give us an allocation which I submit plans for the upcoming year. I say I need to go to Italy for this tour, I then need to go to Switzerland for the World championships. I don’t believe in touring a lot. I like to do my things at home. My athletes are happier doing it this way, we’ve got a great environment here. So we don’t ask for huge amounts of money. We ask for enough to send us overseas 3 times a year, and pay for 3 training camps a year that we do in Lesotho, and Sascoc cover this every season.

V/O: SASCOC is responsible for the preparation and delivery of Team South Africa to the Olympics. Their entire annual budget is R109 million.

Ezera: It is not a lot of money if you compare us with the big Olympic nations in the world who were in the Top 20 at the London Games.

V/O: Ezera Tshabangu is SASCOC’s High Performance Manager.

Ezera: If you look at UK Sport they will give rowing about 32 million pounds, and we only gave Rowing in this financial year ending now about R5.9 million, which is from the allocation we get from the Lotto as SASCOC we still give to some of the federations that are performing.

V/O: While Rowing SA gets R5.9 million a year, British Rowing gets R144 million. That’s more than SASCOC’s entire annual budget.

Devi: How much of your budget is allocated to the athletes?

Ezera: About 56% or so.

Devi: Tell me about Operation Excellence, how much are you spending?

Ezera: We will spend about R30 million a year, of which R12.5 million goes directly to the athletes in terms of their monthly stipends or grants.

V/O: Over the years SASCOC have been criticized for spending too much on themselves, and not enough on the athletes. R14 million goes to employee benefits.

Devi: Do you feel enough is being spent on the athletes? Is the criticism justified?

Ezera: I don’t think it’s justified.

Devi: Right, tell me why?

Ezera: Because obviously it is disclosed, and as I indicated about 56% of the allocations we get go directly to the athletes. If you reduce that or you don’t have people to run the organization, then what happens to the athlete’s support?

V/O: Retired Olympic bronze medalist Ramon di Clemente believes South Africa should be doing more to fund rowing.

Ramon: Olympic champions - what is their worth to our nation? What’s their worth to our kids who aspire to be like them? I think we should re-evaluate that and find a way of supporting them more, and keeping their careers going for as long as possible.

Devi link: A gold medal can be a gateway to fame and fortune, but only for athletes whose chosen sport is popular with large television audiences. Because that’s when the corporate sponsors come flowing in.

Ryk: My life changed - in 3’13” my life changed forever. When I dove into the pool in Athens for the last leg of the relay, I had nothing. I just had enough money to get me to that point, I sold my car, I had no money in the bank. And when I touched my life changed forever. I had all these sponsors, I had an agent and things were really good.

V/O: Ryk Neethling was part of the 4 x 100m freestyle relay team that won gold at the 2004 Olympics. He instantly became a hero and a household name.

Ryk: Corporate South Africa really got behind us, but people think just because you won a gold medal things will change. But it takes a lot of hard work to build a brand. But if you’ve won an Olympic gold medal life definitely gets a bit easier.

V/O: That may be true for gold medalists like Chad le Clos and Cameron van den Burgh, who have both picked up lucrative corporate sponsors. And the professional sportsmen in our national rugby, soccer and cricket teams are all earning at least 2 to 3 million Rand a year.

Roger: I certainly expected corporate South Africa to come to the party and for companies to help us. For companies to pick up an athlete like James Thompson and John Smith who are Olympic champions, world record holders, world champions, what more do we have to do prove ourselves?

V/O: But for Kirsten McCann, the world number 4, lack of funding won’t stop her from chasing the dream.

Kirsten: Olympic gold. I want to be an Olympic champion. I’m in the top four I can get this. I just need to work harder, I need to train harder, and do everything better and I can be a world champion and I can be an Olympic champion. We all know that we’re not going to be driving fancy cars or have a huge amount of excess money, but we’re happy with that. At the end of the day what we want is the gold medal, to be world champion and Olympic champion. That’s what we want.

Roger: I think I’ve got special people in my team. I believe more that people make the difference not money, and if you’ve got the right people in the right place at the right time we can do anything.

Devi: If you got more money would you get better results?

Roger: Some more would definitely help, because we’re on the bottom line. I don’t use any frills. I don’t have any gadgets. I use just a simple coaching watch, my eyes, we have limited resources on video equipment. So if a sponsor came in to help with all of this it would definitely make a difference.
